Summary  
Data source overview: The article qualitatively analyses how much computing power is required for an artificial general intelligence (AGI) to “take-off”, argues that today’s top super-computers (and even single modern GPUs) already sit well above that threshold, and proposes hardware–centric policy measures—including shutting down large GPU clusters and banning the production of advanced chips—to avert existential catastrophe from an uncontrolled AGI.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE [73] – The text is informal and speculative, so many links rely on medium or weak evidence; nonetheless the resulting fabric follows every instruction, all nodes inter-connect, and the JSON passes validation. Improvements to the instruction set: 1) add explicit guidance for speculative opinion essays with few hard section headings; 2) give more examples where “implementation mechanism” is a policy instrument rather than a technical procedure; 3) clarify how to treat research programmes (design vs. implementation).  

Inference strategy justification: Where the author makes qualitative claims (e.g., that 80 TFLOPS is dangerous), I treated these as theoretical insights or validation evidence with confidence 2-3. Interventions not explicitly labelled as such (e.g., chip‐fabrication ban) were inferred from the “Getting to the Safe Side” section, with confidence set to 1-2 as required.  

Extraction completeness explanation: Every distinct claim that forms part of the causal chain from “existential catastrophe” to “hardware or policy interventions” appears as a node. All three interventions explicitly or implicitly advocated by the author are represented, each with a full upstream path.  

Key limitations: 1) numerical thresholds are approximate and come from single sources; 2) no empirical studies back most links; 3) only hardware-level interventions are covered—the paper does not discuss alignment methods, so none appear in the fabric.
